notes: "All the people called out his name." comes right after "Walter ran to his father.", so 'his' could mean Walter or Tell, and 'called out' is a phrasal verb. Clearer: "All the people shouted, 'Tell! Tell!'"
"He put his hat up in the town." does not tell the reader that the hat is on a pole. Clearer: "He put his hat on a long pole in the town." (Quiz Q1 can stay as it is.)
"Put your head down to it!" is a bit stilted as a gloss of 'bow'. Option: "Put your head down in front of it!"
"A bad man named Gessler ruled the land." 'ruled' may be new to some A1 readers, but the next sentence gives enough context. Optional: "Gessler was the boss of the land."
"He looked hard at the apple." A1 readers may take 'hard' to mean 'difficult'. Optional: "He looked at the apple for a long time."
Only a few words are above beginner level (ruled, called out, at last, storm) and none of them block understanding.
"Walter ran to his father, and the people called out his name." has the same unclear 'his' as A1. Option: "...and the people shouted Tell's name."
No conditionals and no passive voice. The imperatives ("Hit it, and you are free.") are fine for B1.
Walter refusing the blindfold, the young nobleman's protest, Gessler coming back from the hunt and the promise to spare Tell's life before he explains the second arrow all match Schiller.

Faithful to Schiller in detail: Walter's boast about the hundred paces leads Gessler to set the test, the linden tree, Tell staying out of the secret oath, and the leap onto the rock shelf in the storm. The prose is literary and not padded.

summary: All five levels tell the legend in the right order (the hat, the apple shot, the second arrow, the arrest, the storm and the leap) with keyed quiz answers that are correct and unambiguous. The only departure from the original is the ending: Gessler flees instead of being shot by Tell at Küssnacht. This counts as acceptable softening for a 4+ app, but the 'second arrow was for you' setup is never paid off (noted, not failed). The A1 and A2 notes are small clarity points.
